notes.title: Select functional APIs by contract, not just matching shapes
notes.core: Expose the smallest familiar functional signature that conveys intent. Standard interfaces improve interoperability, while domain-specific contracts justify named interfaces with validation, documentation, and default composition operations.
rules: Start with Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier, UnaryOperator, BinaryOperator and the needed Bi* variants; match arity and return shape precisely.
Prefer IntPredicate, ToLongFunction, IntUnaryOperator or related primitive specializations on hot numeric paths rather than reflexive boxed Function<Integer,Integer>.
Declare a custom functional interface when the contract is domain-specific, requires a checked exception, unusual arity, or useful default operations.
Annotate bespoke single-abstract-method contracts with @FunctionalInterface to detect accidental abstract-method additions.
Do not overload an API with alternative functional interface parameter types when the same lambda could fit more than one overload.
Do not capture a not-yet-constructed object from its own constructor/factory lambda; pass required context as an explicit argument.
nuance: A standard interface may be structurally compatible yet underspecify a domain contract such as comparison ordering or durable side effects.
A primitive specialization can remove boxing, but benchmark allocation and throughput where this matters; interface choice alone is not proof of speed.
Checked exceptions need explicit adapters or a named contract; do not silently hide checked failure inside unchecked wrappers.
default/static methods do not add new abstract obligations to functional interface shape; methods equivalent to public Object members do not count.
Java 21 has more Stream operations and APIs than the publication-era book; verify current API candidates before inventing abstractions.
notes.misconception: If two SAM signatures match, their names, contracts, overload behavior and boxing costs are interchangeable.
notes.production_context: An alerting pipeline takes an IntPredicate for numeric thresholds, Predicate<Alert> for semantic filters, and a named RetryDecision contract for documented escalation rules.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 retains @FunctionalInterface, target typing and overload ambiguity. Use Java 21 JDK docs for modern specializations and APIs; avoid freezing the book-era interface inventory.

notes.title: Streams are a readability tool, not a universal loop replacement
notes.core: Use short, intention-revealing stream pipelines for bulk transformations; keep stateful, control-flow-heavy or diagnostic tasks in loops or named helpers. Streams evaluate lazily and are consumable only once.
rules: Intermediate operations do not execute in the absence of a terminal operation; avoid relying on map or peek for side effects.
Prefer a named transformation to nested lambda machinery that hides intent, input types, ordering or failure handling.
Keep early exit, labeled break, mutable local coordination and complex checked-exception paths in explicit loops where clearer.
Use flatMap when each input yields zero-to-many results rather than accidentally producing nested streams.
Close I/O-backed streams with try-with-resources; neither collect nor count automatically closes file descriptors.
Use typed primitive streams with care: String.chars() yields UTF-16 code units as int, not Unicode code points or characters as a char stream.
nuance: A terminal short-circuit may skip upstream operations; do not use pipeline side effects to enforce must-run audit actions.
A stream cannot be consumed twice; return a supplier if you need repeated traversals from a regenerable source.
toList() returns an unmodifiable List in Java 21; Collectors.toList() does not promise a specific implementation or mutability.
For supplementary Unicode characters use codePoints() when processing code points, not chars() blindly.
Efficiency and clarity can favor a hybrid design: bounded loop for accumulation, stream for post-processing.
notes.misconception: Replacing every loop with one stream chain always reduces complexity and preserves control flow.
notes.production_context: A merchant settlement import reads a bounded file once, closes the file stream, groups valid rows with a named key function, and reports failures explicitly.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 Stream.toList, mapMulti, takeWhile/dropWhile and newer collectors differ from Java 8/9 descriptions; use version-aware return-mutation tests.

notes.title: Make stream reductions data transformations rather than hidden mutations
notes.core: Favor stateless non-interfering mapper/reducer functions and designed collectors. Make duplicate-key decisions, ordering, grouping and mutability explicit rather than using forEach to update shared maps.
rules: Prefer groupingBy, mapping and downstream counting to imperative mutations from forEach.
Specify duplicate-key policy with toMap merge function when collisions are possible; two-argument toMap rejects duplicates.
Use associative reducers and compatible combiners for a reduction that may run in parallel.
Keep record creation, auditing and external requests outside intermediate stream operations unless semantics explicitly permit side effects.
Choose toCollection when output type/mutability is contractually important; avoid depending on unspecified collector map/list implementations.
Use joining for textual aggregation when delimiters and escaping requirements are explicit; it is not automatically a CSV serializer.
nuance: A collector can be mutable internally and still be correct; "side-effect-free" concerns user-supplied functions interfering with stream source or shared state.
toMap merge functions may run in varying combination orders on unordered or parallel streams; nonassociative last-write-wins is not generally deterministic.
groupingByConcurrent and toConcurrentMap offer concurrent accumulation behavior but do not imply ordering or universal performance wins.
Collectors.toUnmodifiableList rejects null elements, whereas Stream.toList may contain null; APIs should state null policy.
Collectors.counting is usually useful downstream; direct stream.count handles a single entire stream.
notes.misconception: A parallel stream and a shared HashMap updated in forEach are equivalent to a collector.
notes.production_context: A transaction-reconciliation service aggregates statuses with deterministic duplicate handling and publishes idempotent updates only after collecting the result.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 Stream.toList and unmodifiable collectors have distinct null/mutability contracts; standard collectors evolved since the book.

notes.title: Sequence APIs should accommodate traversal and streaming without surprise costs
notes.core: Return a Collection when finite feasible elements can be materialized or represented safely as a collection, enabling both for-each and streaming. Favor Stream or Iterable when laziness, huge cardinality or resource ownership makes Collection misleading.
rules: Prefer Collection or an appropriate List/Set when callers need both enhanced for iteration and stream pipelines.
Avoid materializing huge or potentially unbounded sequences solely to satisfy a Collection signature.
If a sequence has expensive or undefined contains/size operations, a Stream or Iterable may be a more honest API.
Document ownership and closure for resource-backed Stream returns; a caller should know who closes and when.
Do not return a consumed stream or imply that one Stream instance supports repeat traversal.
For lazy collection views, preserve size/contains/get contracts and guard against integer overflow or mutable backing-state surprises.
nuance: Collection.size() is capped at int; extremely large virtual sequences may require alternate interfaces or saturated size semantics.
Collection.stream() is a convenient bridge, but an Iterable alone needs StreamSupport or a dedicated adapter.
Array-backed and specialized collections may be fine for primitives or performance-sensitive cases.
Java 21 SequencedCollection adds encounter-order operations for certain collections; it does not make Stream a Collection.
A returned List of slices may retain a large original backing List, impacting memory lifetime even without copying.
notes.misconception: Returning Stream from every public sequence API automatically supports both stream and for-each users.
notes.production_context: A paginated ledger API returns a small immutable List for a response page and a closeable Stream only for an internal cursor-backed export.
notes.java21_delta: Stream still does not extend Iterable in Java 21. SequencedCollection is new, but resource-backed and unbounded return-type decisions remain.

notes.title: Parallel streams require proven correctness and measured speedup
notes.core: Treat parallel() as a speculative performance change: prove the pipeline remains correct, has sufficient work per splittable unit, and beats a measured sequential baseline under production-like contention.
rules: Do not automatically parallelize unsplittable/infinite or heavily short-circuiting pipelines; they may severely degrade or stall.
Require stateless non-interfering work and associative reductions; mutable shared counters break safety.
Use forEachOrdered if encounter-order output is required, understanding its parallel overhead.
Measure real latency/throughput at representative input sizes and concurrent load, not a single cold timing.
Consider spliterator splitting efficiency, locality, blocking tasks and common fork-join pool interference.
Specify workload thresholds and fallback strategy; a parallel run may lose to sequential for small batches.
nuance: A correctly parallelizable reduction can still be slower because scheduling, combining, allocation or cache misses dominate.
findAny may return different matching elements on parallel streams; findFirst preserves encounter order at potential cost.
A parallel forEach does not promise encounter order; a nonconcurrent collection should not be mutated from multiple callbacks.
The example timings and CPU percentages in the publication are machine/workload observations, not guaranteed Java 21 results.
Benchmark a realistic deployment alongside other fork-join workloads; one pipeline can disturb unrelated requests.
notes.misconception: Adding parallel() guarantees a faster pipeline and preserves iteration order by default.
notes.production_context: A nightly risk analysis tests a pure CPU-intensive aggregation sequentially and in parallel with workload controls; the API server path stays sequential until verified.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 fork-join scheduling, hardware, JDK implementations and vectorization differ from the book-era environment; no fixed speedup or CPU figure is portable.
